Introduction to loadflex

Alison Appling

13 October, 2026

Source: vignettes/intro_to_loadflex.Rmd
intro_to_loadflex.Rmd

The loadflex package lets you quickly fit and compare concentrations and/or fluxes of solutes in watersheds. This vignette demonstrates the application of loadflex to fit four different model types to the same data, to assess and compare those models, and to estimate average solute concentrations and fluxes at both quarter-hourly and monthly scales.

We will use the data supplied with the loadflex package. These include nitrate concentration observations from the Lamprey River in southeastern New Hampshire, where researchers in the NH Water Resources Research Center (University of New Hampshire; PI: William H. McDowell) have been monitoring water quality weekly since 1999. Discharge data are from the same location, Packers Falls, from a USGS gaging station (https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-01073500).

Start by loading the package.

library(loadflex)

Load the data provided in this package.

# Interpolation data: Packers Falls NO3 grab sample observations
data(lamprey_nitrate)
intdat <- lamprey_nitrate[c("DATE","DISCHARGE","NO3")]

# Calibration data: Restrict to points separated by sufficient time
regdat <- subset(lamprey_nitrate, REGR)[c("DATE","DISCHARGE","NO3")]

# Estimation data: Packers Falls discharge
data(lamprey_discharge)
estdat <- subset(lamprey_discharge, DATE < as.POSIXct("2012-10-01 00:00:00", tz="EST5EDT"))
estdat <- estdat[seq(1, nrow(estdat), by=96/4),] # pare to 4 obs/day for speed

Create a metadata description of the dataset & desired output.

meta <- metadata(constituent="NO3", flow="DISCHARGE", 
  dates="DATE", conc.units="mg L^-1", flow.units="cfs", load.units="kg", 
  load.rate.units="kg d^-1", site.name="Lamprey River, NH",
  consti.name="Nitrate", site.id='01073500', lat=43.10259, lon=-70.95256)

Fit four models: interpolation, linear, rloadest, and composite. Many variants on these models are possible. For example: loadInterp models may use any of several interp.fun options; see ?interpolations. loadLm accepts any linear model acceptable to lm(), not just the very simple formula we have used here. loadReg2 functions are also flexible as specified in the documentation for . loadComp models accept a linear model as fit by either loadLm or loadReg2 and any of the interp.fun options available to loadInterp.

no3_li <- loadInterp(interp.format = "conc", interp.fun = rectangularInterpolation, 
  data = intdat, metadata = meta)
no3_lm <- loadLm(formula = log(NO3) ~ log(DISCHARGE), pred.format = "conc", 
  data = regdat, metadata = meta, retrans = exp)
library(rloadest)
no3_lr <- loadReg2(loadReg(NO3 ~ model(9), data = regdat,
  flow = "DISCHARGE", dates = "DATE", time.step = "instantaneous", 
  flow.units = "cfs", conc.units = "mg/L", load.units = "kg",
  station='Lamprey River, NH'))
no3_lc <- loadComp(reg.model = no3_lr, interp.format = "conc", 
  interp.data = intdat, store = c("data", "fitting.function", "uncertainty"))

You can inspect these models in a variety of model-specific ways. Here are some commands to try:

getMetadata(no3_li)
## Metadata for a load model
## -NAME-       -VALUE-
## constituent  NO3
## consti.name  Nitrate
## flow         DISCHARGE
## load.rate    
## dates        DATE
## conc.units   mg L^-1
## flow.units   ft^3 s^-1
## load.units   kg
## load.rate.units kg d^-1
## station      
## site.name    Lamprey River, NH
## site.id      01073500
## lat          43.10259
## lon          -70.95256
## basin.area   NA
## flow.site.name 
## flow.site.id 
## flow.lat     NA
## flow.lon     NA
## flow.basin.area NA
## basin.area.units km^2
get('formula', environment(getFittingFunction(no3_lm)))
## log(NO3) ~ log(DISCHARGE)
getFittedModel(no3_lr)

Now generate point predictions from each model.

preds_li <- predictSolute(no3_li, "flux", estdat, se.pred=TRUE)
preds_lm <- predictSolute(no3_lm, "flux", estdat, se.pred=TRUE, lin.or.log="linear")
preds_lr <- predictSolute(no3_lr, "flux", estdat, se.pred=TRUE)
preds_lc <- predictSolute(no3_lc, "flux", estdat, se.pred=TRUE)

A few lines from one of the resulting prediction data.frames:

head(preds_lr)
##                  date     flux  se.pred
## 1 1999-10-01 01:00:00 15.72780 4.722913
## 2 1999-10-01 07:00:00 16.68311 5.010515
## 3 1999-10-01 13:00:00 17.39594 5.225214
## 4 1999-10-01 19:00:00 16.94764 5.090053
## 5 1999-10-02 01:00:00 16.72981 5.024355
## 6 1999-10-02 07:00:00 16.51078 4.958313

The loadflex process for aggregation of point predictions (to monthly, annual, etc.) has changed since we published our 2015 manuscript. aggregateSolute from that manuscript is no longer exported as a function in loadflex. Instead, you can use the agg.by argument to predictSolute to generate predictions at the time interval of interest.

You can aggregate for for months, water years, calendar years, or other time intervals, and for mean concentration (named conc in the output) or flux (flux.rate in the output, using “rate” to remind users that the time denominator does not change regardless of the time period being aggregated over).

Standard errors (se.fit and se.pred) are available for loadReg2 flux models (but see https://github.com/USGS-R/rloadest/issues/30 and https://github.com/DOI-USGS/loadflex/issues/262). loadReg2 conc models also support aggregation, but only to day.

The units of the aggregated output are what you passed into each model as metadata. count reports the number of observations going into the aggregated estimate in each row. Some examples:

getUnits(getMetadata(no3_lr), 'conc')
## [1] "mg L^-1"
agg_c_li <- predictSolute(no3_li, "conc", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "water year")
agg_c_lm <- predictSolute(no3_lm, "conc", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "calendar year")
agg_c_lr <- predictSolute(no3_lr, "conc", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "day", se.fit = TRUE, se.pred = TRUE)
agg_c_lc <- predictSolute(no3_lc, "conc", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "month")

getUnits(getMetadata(no3_lr), 'flux rate')
## [1] "kg d^-1"
agg_f_li <- predictSolute(no3_li, "flux", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "day")
agg_f_lm <- predictSolute(no3_lm, "flux", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "water year")
agg_f_lr <- predictSolute(no3_lr, "flux", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "month", se.fit = TRUE, se.pred = TRUE)
agg_f_lc <- predictSolute(no3_lc, "flux", newdata = estdat, agg.by = "total")
